raw_text:
Peripartum cardiomyopathy (PPCM) is an idiopathic, pregnancy-associated heart failure syndrome characterized by new left ventricular (LV) systolic dysfunction, typically left ventricular ejection fraction (LVEF) <45%, arising toward the end of pregnancy or in the months after delivery and not explained by another cardiac disorder. Historical criteria restricted onset to the last month of pregnancy through 5 months postpartum, whereas contemporary definitions emphasize exclusion of alternative causes and recognition that presentation may occur across a broader peripartum window [1–4]. PPCM is clinically important because dyspnea, edema, fatigue, orthopnea, and tachycardia overlap with normal pregnancy and puerperium, delaying diagnosis; echocardiography remains central to confirming reduced LVEF and assessing LV size, right ventricular involvement, valvular regurgitation, pulmonary pressures, and intracardiac thrombus [5–7].

The reported incidence varies widely by geography, ascertainment, and case definition. In the United States, administrative and cohort studies suggest increasing recognition over time, with disproportionate burden among Black women and associations with older maternal age, hypertensive disorders of pregnancy, pre-eclampsia/eclampsia, multiple gestation, anemia, obesity, and socioeconomic disadvantage [8–10]. Prospective data from the North American IPAC cohort showed substantial recovery overall but persistent risk in women presenting with severe LV dysfunction or marked LV dilation [11]. The ESC EORP registry broadened this perspective internationally, demonstrating heterogeneity in presentation, treatment, thromboembolic events, and recovery across regions; 1-year data confirmed that mortality and incomplete LV recovery remain clinically relevant despite modern care [12,13].

Pathogenesis is multifactorial. The prolactin hypothesis arose from experimental work showing that oxidative stress and cathepsin D cleavage generate a 16-kDa prolactin fragment with antiangiogenic and proapoptotic effects [14]. Complementary work supports PPCM as a vascular disease: late gestation is an antiangiogenic state, amplified by pre-eclampsia and multiple gestation, with soluble fms-like tyrosine kinase-1 (sFlt1) and impaired myocardial angiogenic reserve implicated in susceptibility [15,16]. Genetic predisposition is increasingly recognized; truncating variants, particularly in TTN, occur in a subset of PPCM patients and overlap with dilated cardiomyopathy, supporting genetic testing when there is severe disease, incomplete recovery, arrhythmia, family history, or recurrent cardiomyopathy [17–19]. Inflammation, immune activation, iron deficiency, fibrosis markers, and cathepsin-D biology may further modify phenotype and prognosis, although few biomarkers beyond natriuretic peptides are ready for routine clinical use [20–23].

Initial evaluation should be urgent in any late-pregnancy or postpartum patient with disproportionate dyspnea, orthopnea, pulmonary edema, hypoxemia, syncope, chest pain, new murmur, arrhythmia, or elevated BNP/NT-proBNP. Differential diagnoses include pre-eclampsia-related pulmonary edema, pulmonary embolism, acute coronary syndrome or spontaneous coronary artery dissection, valvular disease, congenital heart disease, myocarditis, sepsis, thyroid disease, Takotsubo syndrome, and previously unrecognized familial dilated cardiomyopathy [4–7]. Cardiac magnetic resonance can help when diagnosis is uncertain or recovery is incomplete, although gadolinium is generally avoided during pregnancy and used selectively postpartum. Endomyocardial biopsy is not routine, but may be considered for fulminant, treatment-refractory, or atypical presentations when myocarditis, infiltrative disease, or other specific diagnoses would change therapy.

Management requires a cardio-obstetrics team. During pregnancy, treatment follows heart failure principles using fetal-compatible therapies: loop diuretics for congestion, beta-blockers such as metoprolol when tolerated, hydralazine/nitrates for afterload reduction, digoxin in selected cases, and anticoagulation when LVEF is severely reduced or thrombus is present. Angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitors, angiotensin receptor blockers, angiotensin receptor–neprilysin inhibitors, mineralocorticoid receptor antagonists, and sodium–glucose cotransporter-2 inhibitors are avoided during pregnancy but are generally considered postpartum as compatible with standard heart failure therapy depending on lactation, renal function, blood pressure, and drug-specific safety. Delivery timing is individualized; vaginal delivery with regional anesthesia is preferred when maternal status is stable, whereas hemodynamic instability, refractory hypoxemia, or obstetric indications may require expedited delivery in a monitored setting [4,5].

Bromocriptine, which suppresses prolactin release, is the most studied disease-specific therapy. A small proof-of-concept randomized study and a subsequent multicenter randomized trial suggested favorable recovery rates when bromocriptine was added to standard therapy, but the evidence base remains limited, and therapy requires lactation cessation and attention to thrombosis risk, usually with anticoagulation [24–26]. Cohort comparisons suggest that access to guideline-directed medical therapy, anticoagulation, bromocriptine protocols, and advanced heart failure care may influence outcomes [27]. Mechanical circulatory support or transplantation is reserved for cardiogenic shock or refractory end-stage disease, with recognition that myocardial recovery may occur even after severe presentation.

Counseling after recovery is essential. Subsequent pregnancy carries risk of recurrent LV dysfunction, heart failure, fetal complications, and death, especially when LVEF has not normalized before conception; even women with apparent recovery require preconception evaluation, shared decision-making, and close surveillance with serial echocardiography and natriuretic peptides [28–30]. Long-term follow-up is recommended because relapse, persistent remodeling, arrhythmias, psychosocial morbidity, and uncertainty about medication withdrawal remain unresolved. Future priorities include earlier diagnosis, equitable access to cardio-obstetric care, validated biomarkers, genotype-informed risk stratification, and adequately powered trials of targeted therapies.
